subject: chemistry
title: Chemical cells and batteries
key_idea: A chemical cell uses a chemical reaction to produce a voltage. The voltage depends on the electrodes and the electrolyte. A non-rechargeable cell stops working when one reactant is used up.

blocks.text: (Separate science) This section covers what a cell contains and what decides its voltage.

items.meaning: A device in which chemicals react to produce electricity.
A piece of metal dipped in the electrolyte.
A solution that the electrodes are placed in.
Two or more cells connected together in series.

items: A simple cell is made by connecting two **different metals** in contact with an electrolyte.
The voltage depends on the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte.
Other factors, such as the temperature or the concentration of the electrolyte, can also change the voltage.
The bigger the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage.
Two electrodes made of the same metal give a voltage of 0 V.
Against a fixed reference electrode, the higher the positive voltage, the more reactive the metal. A negative voltage means the metal is less reactive than the reference.
Electrolysis uses electricity to produce a chemical reaction.
A chemical cell uses a chemical reaction to produce electricity.
A simple cell needs two different metals and an electrolyte.
A greater difference in reactivity gives a greater voltage.

blocks.text: (Separate science) Cells in series add their voltages to give a battery with a greater voltage.

blocks.label: Voltage of a battery
blocks.formula: battery voltage = number of cells × voltage of one cell
where: the cells are connected in series and have the same voltage
voltage of one cell is in V

items.text: To make a 12 V battery from 1.5 V cells, number of cells = 12 ÷ 1.5.

diagram.alt: Work out the voltage of a battery made from cells in series.
diagram.question: A battery has {n} cells connected in series. Each cell has a voltage of {v} V. Calculate the voltage of the battery.
working: Battery voltage = number of cells × voltage of one cell

items: A battery is two or more cells connected in series.
Add the voltages of the cells to find the battery voltage.

blocks.text: (Separate science) A chemical cell produces a voltage until one of its reactants is used up.

diagram.alt: Voltage of a non-rechargeable cell over time: constant, then falling to zero as a reactant is used up.

items: In a **non-rechargeable** cell the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.
A torch or bulb powered by such a cell starts bright, becomes dimmer and then goes out.
A non-rechargeable cell cannot be recharged because the reaction is not reversible.
A **rechargeable** cell can be recharged. When an external electrical current is supplied, the chemical reactions are reversed.

rows: Does not have to be thrown away

items: Reactions in a non-rechargeable cell stop when a reactant is used up, and the voltage falls to 0 V.
A rechargeable cell works again because an external current reverses the reactions.

checks.q: (Separate science) Why do alkaline batteries eventually stop working?
checks.a: One of the reactants is used up and the reaction stops.

checks.q: (Separate science) How many 1.5 V cells in series are needed to make a 12 V battery?
(Separate science) Why does a cell with two copper electrodes in an electrolyte give a voltage of 0 V?
checks.a: Two different metals are needed to produce a voltage. Both electrodes are the same metal, so there is no difference in reactivity.

worked_example.question:
A student investigated the voltage produced by different pairs of metal electrodes in a chemical cell.

The student placed a nickel electrode and an electrode made from a different metal (electrode A) in 1.0 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solution and measured the voltage. This was repeated using different metals for electrode A.

Electrode A and voltage in volts:
Copper (Cu): −0.59
Magnesium (Mg): 2.12
Nickel (Ni): 0.00
Silver (Ag): −1.05
Zinc (Zn): 0.51

Write the symbols of the five metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.

Justify your answer.
answer_points: Order: Mg, Zn, Ni, Cu, Ag (most reactive to least reactive).
Justification: the higher the (positive) voltage, the more reactive the metal.
(The most reactive metal has the highest voltage and the least reactive the most negative voltage.)
worked_example.tip: Two marks for the order and one for the justification. Naming the metals instead of the symbols is allowed.

worked_example.question:
Chemical cells produce a voltage.

A chemical cell can be made by placing the metals copper and iron in a beaker of sodium chloride solution. A voltmeter is connected to the metals.

Describe what will happen to the reading on the voltmeter over a long period of time.
worked_example.tip: The marks are independent. Give the pattern in order: constant, then decrease, then zero.

worked_example.question:
Which statement about chemical cells is correct?

A They produce a voltage indefinitely.
B They produce a voltage once all of the reactants are used up.
C They produce a voltage until one of the reactants is completely used up.
D They produce a voltage until the reactants are partly used up.
answer_points: C: they produce a voltage until one of the reactants is completely used up.
A is wrong because a cell cannot produce a voltage forever.
B is wrong because no voltage is produced once the reactants are used up.
D is wrong because the cell keeps working until a reactant is completely used up, not partly.
worked_example.tip: Pick the statement that says the voltage lasts until a reactant is completely used up.
